passage:
"Look at this!" Omkar held the phone out across the canteen table. "The constable told me to move my bike and I said, 'Do what you want.' Look at the views!"
Hemant watched the clip twice. Part of Hemant wanted those views too.
"You should try it next time we get stopped," Omkar said. "Just act bold."
"Weren't you scared? Your voice went up at the end."
"A bit."
"That's what I'm thinking about," Hemant said. "Staying calm would've taken more nerve. If it goes wrong, nobody in the comments walks into the station with you."
Omkar shrugged and pulled the phone back. "Maybe." But the phone stayed face down for the rest of lunch.

qa.q: What did Omkar say to the constable, according to the story?
qa.a: Omkar said, "Do what you want."

qa.q: What does Hemant feel while watching the clip, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Hemant feels a pull to copy; the passage says part of Hemant wanted those views too, yet Hemant asks about the fear in Omkar's voice.

qa.q: What could Hemant say next time a friend pushes to film a stand-off?
qa.a: That staying calm and safe matters more than views, and that the comments will not help if things go wrong.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel about Hemant's comment?
qa.a: A little defensive but also thoughtful; admitting "A bit" and leaving the phone face down suggest the words landed.

grounding: A friend brags about talking back to police for a video; Hemant feels the pull to copy and chooses calm over likes.

passage:
Gautam had been pacing the hall since the phone call from the school gate. Jaya came in, bag still on one shoulder.
"From tomorrow you come straight home. No cycling around with friends."
"Papa, please sit. Let me tell you everything."
"Everything? A policeman held you!"
"Two constables asked three of us about a stolen bicycle near the ground. I gave my name and school. They checked, and we were let go. That's all."
Gautam's hands shook a little. "When they rang, I imagined the worst. I couldn't breathe."
"I know, Papa. I was scared too. But if you shut me in, I'll stop telling you things."
Gautam sat down slowly. "Then what do you want?"
"I'll share my location, and message when I reach school and home. Will that help?"
"Yes. That I can live with."

qa.q: What were the constables asking about?
qa.a: They were asking about a stolen bicycle near the ground.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Gautam was frightened; the pacing, the shaking hands and "I imagined the worst" show it.

qa.q: What made this conversation work?
qa.a: Jaya listened to the fear, told the full story and offered concrete habits, sharing the location and messaging on arrival, which gave Gautam something safe to hold on to. ❤️

qa.q: What would have changed if Jaya had simply stormed off?
qa.a: Gautam's fear would probably have stayed and the strict rule too; Jaya even says that being shut in would end the telling.

grounding: A parent frightened by a police questioning turns strict; Jaya listens, shares the full story and agrees on safe habits.

passage: Rashmi, you asked how I cope at prayer time with Dadi when I'm unsure about half of it. Let me tell you what I did at fifteen. I'm Jeevan, and I had stopped believing in some of the rituals. Every evening Dadi lit the lamp and sang, and I sat beside her with my shoes off. I didn't mock. I didn't pretend either; inside, I stayed honest. Once she asked, "Do you believe like me?" I said, "Not the same way, Dadi, but I love sitting here with you." She patted my knee and kept singing. Years later I remember her songs better than most lessons.

qa.q: How old was Jeevan when this happened?
qa.a: Jeevan was fifteen.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling as Jeevan sat beside Dadi?
qa.a: Love for Dadi together with honest doubt inside; Jeevan stayed beside Dadi but did not pretend to believe everything.

qa.q: How can someone with doubts still honour a grandparent's faith?
qa.a: Sit beside the grandparent, listen, do not mock, and be gently honest if asked, as Jeevan did.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt when Jeevan said "Not the same way"?
qa.a: Perhaps a little sad, but also comforted by the love; she patted Jeevan's knee and kept singing.

grounding: Jeevan loses belief in some rituals but sits beside the grandmother at prayer out of love while staying honest inside.

passage:
After Friday prayers, Irfan and Abhinav took their tea to the low wall by the corner stall.
"You told me last week you don't get some of the rules," Abhinav said. "So why go every Friday?"
"Because it's home. Rahim Uncle saves my spot. The boys are there. Ammi's sheer khurma on Eid. When I was small, the smell of that carpet meant safe."
"And the questions?"
"I ask them. I asked our imam about one thing and he said, 'Good question, come Sunday and we'll talk.' He wasn't angry."
"So you don't have to pick."
Irfan turned the glass in his hands. "I keep waiting to be afraid of picking. I'm just not."

qa.q: Who saves Irfan's spot at the mosque?
qa.a: Rahim Uncle saves Irfan's spot.

qa.q: What is Irfan feeling toward the mosque, and what shows it?
qa.a: Irfan feels belonging and warmth, shown by "it's home" and the memory of the carpet smelling safe, while still holding real questions.

qa.q: What would you advise a friend who wants both belonging and questions?
qa.a: Keep going to the place that feels like home, and ask the questions to an elder or friend who welcomes them, without fearing either.

qa.q: How does Abhinav see Irfan's stance?
qa.a: With curiosity; Abhinav asks why Irfan goes despite the doubts and ends up saying Irfan does not have to pick.

grounding: Irfan finds friends and a sense of home at the mosque and still asks questions, keeping both without fear.

passage:
Dear Abhinav,
I'm writing because I can't say this out loud. Last week at the youth circle I asked why one rule is followed the way it is. I wasn't mocking anything; I really wanted to know. Two elders said I was disrespectful, and since then people look away when I walk in. Nobody sits with me. It hurts far more than I expected, and I keep thinking of quitting altogether. But yesterday my Nana's old friend, Mr Fazal, said, "A question is not an insult." I nearly cried with relief. Maybe those two elders are not the whole community. Thank you for not laughing when I told you.
Yusuf

qa.q: What happened after Yusuf asked the question at the youth circle?
qa.a: Two elders called Yusuf disrespectful, and people started looking away when Yusuf walked in.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling after being shunned, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Yusuf was deeply hurt and isolated; "It hurts far more than I expected" and "Nobody sits with me" show it. 🤍

qa.q: What could Yusuf do next?
qa.a: Keep talking with open-minded people such as Mr Fazal and Abhinav, and remember that two elders are not the whole community.

qa.q: How might the two elders have seen Yusuf's question?
qa.a: As disrespect toward what they hold dear; they called it disrespectful, though Yusuf says it was honest curiosity.

grounding: Yusuf asks a doubtful question, is shunned and hurt by elders, and finds an open-minded elder without treating the group as the whole faith.

passage: Jahnavi, you asked why I stopped going to the prayer room, so here it is. I'm Akash. When Dada died in March, I was furious with God for letting it happen. Really angry. I'd lie awake asking, "Where were you?" I wrote it in a notebook so Mummy wouldn't hear. Part of me thought, if I'm this angry, I must still think someone is there to be angry at. Then I wasn't sure of anything. My friend Fayaz doesn't believe in God, and he told me he was furious at the universe when his aunt died. So it isn't only believers. I'm still angry, but I've stopped hiding it.

qa.q: When did Akash's Dada die?
qa.a: Dada died in March.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling toward God, and how did Akash express it?
qa.a: Akash felt angry and let down, asking "Where were you?" at night and writing it in a notebook. 🤍

qa.q: What could Akash do with the anger?
qa.a: Keep saying or writing it honestly, and share it with a friend like Jahnavi or a trusted adult instead of hiding it.

qa.q: How does Fayaz see anger after a loss?
qa.a: Fayaz was furious at the universe when his aunt died, so Fayaz sees it as something believers and non-believers both feel.

grounding: After a loss Akash is angry at God and speaks it aloud, learning that believers and non-believers both feel such anger.

passage: In their small town by the river, Elizabeth practised one sentence for a week with Salma on the walk home from school. "Not in the middle of dinner," Salma said. "Pick a calm time." So on Sunday afternoon, when the plates were washed and the fan hummed, Elizabeth sat with Mama and Papa on the verandah. "I need to tell you something. I don't believe the way you do anymore. I still love and respect you, and I'll come to church with you at Christmas. I'm not asking you to agree." Papa looked at his hands. Mama said, "Give us time." It wasn't acceptance, but nobody shouted. Elizabeth breathed out and went to make tea for everyone.

qa.q: When did Elizabeth speak to Mama and Papa?
qa.a: On Sunday afternoon, when the plates were washed and the fan hummed.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth want from this talk, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Elizabeth wanted to be honest while keeping the respect, shown by the week of practice and "I'm not asking you to agree".

qa.q: What could Elizabeth do in the coming weeks?
qa.a: Keep joining family events honestly, such as church at Christmas, stay respectful and give Mama and Papa time. 🙂

qa.q: How might Mama and Papa be feeling?
qa.a: Probably worried or sad: Papa looked at his hands and Mama asked for time, but neither shouted.

grounding: Elizabeth tells the parents at a calm time that belief has changed, says respect remains and does not demand acceptance.

passage: I'm Wasim, and I live next door to Suraj, so I hear things through the wall. Last Sunday Suraj's father said, quite loudly, "Who will carry these customs after us?" Suraj's mother looked close to tears. Suraj didn't argue. Suraj said, "I hear you. I'm still coming to the festival dinner and helping with the lamps, I just can't say the words the way I used to." Then I saw Suraj carry the lamps to the courtyard and stand with the family, quiet. I can't tell what Suraj really feels: maybe sad, maybe relieved. Later Suraj's father passed Suraj the sweets. Nobody said much, but it wasn't a fight.

qa.q: What did Suraj's father ask loudly?
qa.a: Suraj's father asked, "Who will carry these customs after us?"

qa.q: What might Suraj be feeling, and why is Wasim unsure?
qa.a: Suraj may be sad or relieved; Wasim only sees behaviour, such as the quiet and the lamps, not the inner state.

qa.q: What could Suraj do in the months ahead?
qa.a: Keep hearing the parents' fear, keep joining the family events that can be joined honestly, and let time do its work.

qa.q: How does Suraj's father see the situation?
qa.a: With fear that the family's traditions may not be passed on, which is why he asks who will carry them.

grounding: Suraj's parents fear the traditions will not be passed on; Suraj hears them and stays part of family events honestly.

passage: I'm Pooja, and I sit behind Irfan in assembly. Irfan doesn't say the prayer and doesn't make trouble, just stands with hands folded. At lunch, only to me, Irfan said, "There's no god for me, and it feels lonely. Everyone just assumes." I said nothing clever. I moved my tiffin closer. Later in the library Irfan showed me a book on stars and said, "When I read this I feel small in a good way." I also saw Irfan help the caretaker carry chairs without being asked. I can't say the loneliness is gone, but Irfan asked if I'd come to the astronomy club on Friday.

qa.q: What did Irfan show Pooja in the library?
qa.a: Irfan showed Pooja a book on stars.

qa.q: What does Irfan feel about not believing, and how does Pooja know?
qa.a: Irfan feels lonely, because Irfan said so at lunch, and also a sense of awe when reading about the stars.

qa.q: What could Irfan do to feel less alone?
qa.a: Find people, books and values to rely on, such as the astronomy club, and keep the kindness that already shows in helping.

qa.q: How might Pooja's moving the tiffin closer matter to Irfan?
qa.a: It may have shown company without judgement, though Pooja cannot be sure how it felt to Irfan.

grounding: Irfan feels lonely in not believing in any god, and an observer sees awe, ethics and a first move toward people who share Irfan's interests.

passage:
At the school canteen, Urmila unwrapped her lunch. "Can I ask you something? Why do you fast at this time of year, and what's it like?"
Darshan thought. "Hard on the first day, then quiet. It makes me think about people who don't have enough. Why do you light a lamp at home every evening?"
"Habit at first," Urmila said. "Now it's the only quiet minute in the house."
"Do you believe it does something?"
"I'm not sure. I believe in the minute."
Neither tried to win. When the bell rang, Darshan said, "Come to our festival lunch if you like. No pressure."
Urmila grinned. "And you come to ours."

qa.q: What does Urmila say the lamp gives her at home?
qa.a: Urmila says it is the only quiet minute in the house.

qa.q: What does Urmila want in asking Darshan these questions, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Urmila wants to understand out of curiosity, not to argue; the polite "Can I ask you something?" and the open listening show it.

qa.q: What makes this conversation work?
qa.a: Both listen to learn instead of trying to win or convert, and both answer honestly, even about doubt. 😊

qa.q: How might Darshan feel about being asked?
qa.a: Probably glad to be treated with curiosity and not judged, since Darshan answers openly, asks back and offers an invitation.

grounding: Friends of different religions ask each other real questions, listening to learn and not to win.
